plan.title: Projectile Challenge: Hit the Target
plan.description: A small launcher sits on flat ground with a target standing some distance away. You set the launch angle and speed, press Launch, and the ball flies along a curved path while leaving a dotted trail. If it lands on the target you win. If it misses, the scene shows where it landed and how far short or long it was so you can adjust and try again.
plan.reason: You asked for a game, and a short challenge with a clear target makes you test how angle and speed together decide where the ball lands. Each miss shows its distance from the target, so you can improve your next shot.
interactions: Set the launch angle and launch speed before each shot
Press Launch to fire the ball and watch it fly
Press Reset to bring the ball back and try again
Press New Target to move the target to a different distance
Ask for a hint about whether to aim higher, lower, faster or slower
assumptions: There is no air resistance, so the ball follows a perfect curved path.
The ball launches from ground level and the ground is flat.
Gravity is a constant 9.8 m/s² pulling straight down.
A shot counts as a hit if it lands within half a metre of the target's centre.
limitations: The ball stops where it lands. It does not bounce or roll.
Wind, spin and drag are ignored, so real throws would fall shorter than shown.
plan.learningGoal: See how launch angle and speed together set how far a ball travels, and that two different angles can reach the same distance.

plan.title: Pendulum length and period
plan.description: A bob hangs from a fixed pivot on a string and swings back and forth. As you drag the length slider from 0.5 to 3 metres, the string grows or shrinks and the swing slows down or speeds up. A readout shows the period in seconds, worked out from the length, next to the current length.
plan.reason: You want to change the length and watch the period respond. With one slider, you can see the swing and the period number change together, so you can tell that the period grows with the square root of the length.
interactions: Drag the length slider between 0.5 and 3 metres
Read the period, in seconds, as the length changes
Speed the swing up or slow it down, or pause and scrub through it
Turn the view to see the swing from any side
assumptions: Small swings: the period is 2π times the square root of length divided by g, with g = 9.81 m/s²
The string is light and doesn't stretch, and the bob is treated as a single point
There is no air resistance or friction, so the swing never dies down
The starting angle stays small and fixed
limitations: Large swing angles, where the real period gets a little longer, are not shown
Damping and energy loss are not shown
plan.learningGoal: See that a pendulum's period depends only on its length: making it four times longer doubles the period.

plan.title: Projectile Target Challenge: Pick Angle and Speed
plan.description: A small launcher sits at the left end of a flat 70 m field with distance marks every 10 m, and a flagged target zone sits somewhere down the field. You set the launch angle and speed, then press Launch: the ball flies along its arc while a trail is drawn, and when it lands the card shows how far it went and how far it missed by. Hit three targets, placed at 30 m, 45 m and 18 m in turn, using no more than 10 launches.
plan.reason: This is a game because you asked for one. Aiming, missing and adjusting shows you how angle and speed together decide where the ball lands.
interactions: Set the launch angle: the launcher barrel tilts to match, and the new angle is used on the next launch.
Set the launch speed: the new speed is used on the next launch.
Press Launch: the ball flies its arc over about two seconds, with a trail behind it. The arc from your last shot stays as a faded dashed line so you can compare.
Readouts show the landing distance, how far the shot missed and to which side (short or long), the flight time, the highest point, launches used out of 10, and targets hit out of 3.

A hit is a landing within 1.5 m of the target's centre, counting both edges. After a hit, the target moves to its next position. The game is won after 3 hits and lost if 10 launches are used up first.
Hint: with the same speed, angles that add up to 90° (for example 30° and 60°) land at the same distance, and 45° goes farthest.
assumptions: This is a simplified simulation: no air resistance, and the ball starts at ground level on flat ground.
Gravity is 9.8 m/s² straight down. The ball keeps the same sideways speed and only its vertical speed changes.
Each step of the flight is computed exactly from the projectile formulas, so the landing distance equals speed² × sin(2 × angle) ÷ 9.8.
The ball is treated as a point, and the flight ends the moment it returns to ground height.
The targets come in a fixed order (30 m, 45 m, 18 m), so Reset starts the same challenge again and clears the score and the trails.
limitations: Real balls are slowed by air, so in real life they land shorter than shown, especially at high speeds. The 45° best angle holds exactly only when there is no air resistance.
The longest possible shot is about 64 m (25 m/s at 45°), so every target can be reached, but a slow shot at a very steep or very flat angle lands only a few metres away.
Flight is shown sped up or slowed down to take about two seconds, so the time on screen does not match the flight-time readout.
plan.learningGoal: See how launch angle and speed together set how far a projectile travels: 45° gives the longest shot, two angles that add to 90° land at the same spot, and doubling the speed makes the shot go four times as far.

plan.title: Stochastic gradient descent on a loss bowl: learning rate and batch size
plan.description: A bowl-shaped surface shows the error (loss) of a straight-line fit y = w·x + b for every slope w and intercept b, using a fixed set of 64 made-up data points. A ball marks the current guess and leaves a path as it moves. Each step uses a small random batch of points to estimate the downhill direction, then moves the ball. An arrow shows that batch's step direction and a faint arrow shows the full-data downhill direction for comparison. Change the learning rate and batch size, run the descent, and compare paths that are smooth, noisy, slow or unstable.
plan.reason: You asked to change the learning rate and batch size. Running real step-by-step updates and watching the path on the loss surface shows directly how each setting affects speed, noise and stability.
interactions: Play or step the descent: each step draws a random batch, computes its gradient (the uphill direction of its error) and moves the ball the opposite way by learning rate times gradient.
Learning rate: small values give short, slow steps; middle values tend to zigzag across the bowl; near the top, steps overshoot, the ball leaves the bowl and the run shows 'diverged'.
Batch size: a batch of 1 gives a jittery path because each step's direction varies a lot. A batch of 64 uses all the points, so it follows the full-data downhill direction smoothly.
Action 'Start a new run, keep old path': moves the ball back to the starting point with your current settings and keeps the previous path faded, so you can compare two settings.
Click the ball or the arrows to see what they represent.
assumptions: Real SGD on a small, made-up dataset fitting a straight line. It is not a large neural network.
The loss is mean squared error over the 64 fixed points. The surface shows the full-data loss for each (w, b).
Batches are drawn without repeats within a step, using a fixed random seed. Reset replays the same sequence of batches.
Each run starts from the same point (w, b) away from the minimum. A run ends after 150 steps or when the ball leaves the plotted region.
Readouts: step number, this batch's loss, full-data loss, current w and b, and the length of the step.
limitations: Each step lowers the full-data loss only on average. With small batches, single steps can raise it.
This bowl has one minimum. Real network loss surfaces have many valleys, flat regions and saddle points that this scene does not show.
Momentum, Adam and learning-rate schedules are not included. The learning rate stays fixed during a run.
Where exactly the descent becomes unstable depends on this dataset. The numbers are illustrative and do not apply in general.
plan.learningGoal: SGD follows a noisy estimate of the downhill direction. The learning rate sets how far each step goes and whether the descent stays stable. The batch size sets how noisy each step's direction is.

plan.title: Pendulum length and period
plan.description: A bob hangs on a string from a fixed support and swings back and forth. Use the length slider to set the string anywhere from 0.5 to 3 metres. The swing speeds up or slows down to match, and a number shows the period, which is the time for one full swing there and back.
plan.reason: You want to change the length and see the period change. An experiment lets you move the slider and watch the swing and the period number update together.
interactions: Drag the length slider between 0.5 and 3 metres
Read the period, in seconds, next to the pendulum
Orbit the camera to see the swing from any side
Change the playback speed to compare swings more easily
assumptions: The swing is small, so the period is two pi times the square root of length divided by gravity
Gravity is 9.81 metres per second squared
The string has no mass and does not stretch, and the bob acts like a single point
There is no air resistance or friction, so the swing never dies down
limitations: For large swings the real period is a little longer than the period shown here
The motion is calculated from a formula, not simulated, so it will not show the swing slowing down
plan.learningGoal: The period grows with the square root of the length. Making the pendulum four times longer doubles its period.

plan.title: Reach the Goal: Token on a 3 by 3 Grid
plan.description: A 3 by 3 board of square tiles sits on a table. A round token starts in one corner and a highlighted goal square with a flag is marked in the opposite corner. Use the up, down, left and right buttons to move the token one square at a time. A move counter tracks your steps, and a message tells you when you reach the goal.
plan.reason: You asked for a small game with buttons, a goal, a hint and a reset. A bounded challenge with move buttons and a clear win fits that exactly.
interactions: Press Up, Down, Left or Right to move the token one square
Press Hint to see which direction moves you closer to the goal
Press Reset to put the token back at the start and clear the move counter
Orbit the camera to view the board from any angle
assumptions: The token moves exactly one square per button press and cannot leave the board; a move off the edge is ignored.
The goal stays in the same marked square every round.
The fewest moves to win is 4, and the counter shows how close you came to that.
limitations: The token jumps from square to square. It does not slide smoothly between them.
There are no obstacles or opponents, so the challenge is simple.
plan.learningGoal: See how moves in four directions add up to a path across a grid, and find the shortest route to a target.

plan.title: Stochastic Gradient Descent on a Loss Surface
plan.description: A curved bowl-shaped surface stands for the loss over two model weights, and a ball marks the current weights. Each step, an arrow shows the noisy gradient estimate from a small batch of data, the ball moves downhill by that arrow, and a trail records its path. Change the learning rate and batch size, then compare the paths. Small batches give jittery paths, and a large learning rate makes the ball overshoot, zig-zag or fly off the bowl.
plan.reason: You asked to change the learning rate and batch size and see what happens. A hands-on experiment fits best: you set both values, run the descent step by step and compare the paths and loss readouts.
interactions: Set the learning rate and watch the step length grow or shrink
Choose a batch size and see how noisy the gradient arrow becomes
Take one step at a time to follow each update
Run many steps at once to see the whole path
Reset the ball to the same starting point to compare settings fairly
Orbit the camera to see the path from above or from the side
assumptions: The loss is a smooth stretched bowl with one lowest point, standing in for a real model's loss.
The model has only two weights, so the loss can be drawn as a surface.
Each batch's gradient is the true gradient plus random noise, and the noise shrinks as the batch size grows.
The update is plain gradient descent with no momentum and no learning-rate schedule.
limitations: Real neural network losses have many dimensions, flat regions and multiple valleys, which a single bowl cannot show.
The noise is simulated, not computed from a real dataset.
Training time per step is not modelled, so the speed advantage of small batches does not appear.
plan.learningGoal: See that the learning rate sets how far each update moves, so too large means overshooting, and that smaller batches give noisier gradient estimates and therefore wobblier paths toward the minimum.

plan.title: Projectile Challenge: Hit the Target
plan.description: A small launcher sits at the left end of a flat field, with a target on the ground farther along. You set the launch angle and speed, press Launch, and the ball flies along its curved path, leaving a trail. A hit lights up the target. A miss shows how far short or long the ball landed, so you can adjust and try again.
plan.reason: You asked for a game, and a short challenge where you adjust angle and speed after each miss makes you think about how both settings change the flight path.
interactions: Set the launch angle and launch speed with sliders
Choose how far away the target is
Press Launch to fire the ball and watch its flight
Press Reset to put the ball back on the launcher
Ask for a hint showing which direction to adjust
assumptions: No air resistance, so the ball follows a perfect parabola.
The ball launches from ground level and lands on flat ground.
Gravity is 9.8 m/s² pointing straight down.
The target counts as hit if the ball lands within 1 m of its centre.
limitations: Without air resistance, real balls would fall shorter than shown, especially at high speeds.
The ball does not bounce or roll after it lands.
plan.learningGoal: See how launch angle and speed together decide how far a ball travels, and that two different angles can give the same distance.

plan.title: Projectile Challenge: Hit the Target
plan.description: A small launcher sits at one end of a flat field, and a target ring lies on the ground somewhere between 10 and 35 metres away. You set the launch angle and speed, press Launch, and the ball flies along a curved path while a faint trail traces its flight. When it lands, a label shows hit or miss and how far short or long the ball landed. Hit the target within five tries to win, then move the target and try again.
plan.reason: You asked for a game. Trying to hit a target with a limited number of tries makes you change the angle and speed on purpose and see how each one changes where the ball lands.
interactions: Set the launch angle and launch speed with sliders
Press Launch to fire the ball and watch it fly
Press New Target to move the target to a different distance
Press Reset to start over with five fresh tries
Ask for a hint when stuck
Orbit the camera to view the flight from the side or from behind
assumptions: There is no air resistance, so the ball follows a perfect parabola.
Gravity is 9.8 m/s² and the ground is flat.
The ball launches from ground level, and it counts as a hit if it lands within 1 metre of the target's centre.
The ball stops where it first touches the ground. It does not bounce or roll.
limitations: The flight is calculated from the standard projectile formulas, not simulated with full physics, so there is no spin, wind or bouncing.
Targets are placed only on the ground. There are no raised targets or obstacles.
plan.learningGoal: How the launch angle and speed together set how far a projectile travels, including that 45° gives the longest throw and that pairs of angles adding up to 90° land at the same distance.

plan.title: Simple Pendulum: How Length Sets the Period
plan.description: A bob hangs from a fixed pivot on a thin string and swings back and forth, with a ruler-style marker showing the string length. Slide the length between 0.5 and 3 metres and the string grows or shrinks while the swing visibly slows or speeds up. A readout shows the period in seconds, updated at once, next to the length and the swings per minute.
plan.reason: You want to change one quantity and see a computed result. An experiment card ties the length slider to both the swinging motion and the period number, so you can see and measure the effect together.
interactions: Drag the length slider from 0.5 to 3 metres and watch the swing and the period change
Change the starting swing angle to see that, for small swings, the period barely depends on it
Switch gravity to compare the same pendulum on Earth, the Moon and Mars
Orbit the camera and click the bob or string for its label
Change the playback speed or pause to study one swing
assumptions: The period is calculated with the small-swing formula: period = 2π × √(length ÷ gravity).
The string has no mass and does not stretch, and the bob is treated as a point.
There is no air resistance or friction, so the swing never dies down.
limitations: At larger starting angles a real pendulum takes slightly longer than this formula predicts (about 0.2% longer at 10°). The scene does not show that difference.
The motion is calculated from a formula, not simulated, so damping and wobbling of the string are not shown.
plan.learningGoal: See that a pendulum's period grows with the square root of its length: making it four times longer doubles the period. For small swings, the period does not depend on how wide the swing is.

plan.title: Stochastic Gradient Descent on a Loss Bowl: Learning Rate and Batch Size
plan.description: A ball moves one step at a time down a stretched bowl-shaped surface. The surface is the loss, and its lowest point is the best setting of two model weights. At each step, two arrows appear at the ball: one shows the true downhill direction and one shows the noisy estimate from a small batch. The ball moves along the noisy arrow by a distance set by the learning rate and leaves a short trail. Each run lasts at most 40 steps, so you can quickly see the path change from slow, to wobbly, to smooth, to zig-zag, to blowing up.
plan.reason: You change the two settings you named and watch a short 40-step descent play out differently. The arrows and trail at each step show how a noisy small batch or a large learning rate changes the path.
interactions: Play, pause or step one update at a time. The ball moves once per step and adds one trail point, up to 40 points.
Change the learning rate: tiny values stay far from the bottom after 40 steps; above 0.25 the path zig-zags on the steep side; above 0.5 bounces grow and can end as 'diverged'.
Change the batch size: with 1 example the noisy arrow swings widely and the path jitters near the bottom; bigger batches stay closer to the true arrow; the full batch matches it.
Changing either setting restarts the run from the same starting point.
'Keep this path and run again' turns the current trail (up to 40 points) into a faded comparison path, replacing any earlier one, then starts a new run from the same start.
Orbit the camera to see the bowl from above or from the side.
assumptions: Illustration: a made-up loss bowl for two weights with simulated batch noise, not a real model trained on real data.
The loss is half of (x² + 4y²), so it is 4 times steeper along one weight than the other. Its single lowest point is at the centre.
The batch gradient is the true gradient plus random noise. The noise shrinks as one over the square root of the batch size and is zero for the full batch.
Each update is: new position = old position − learning rate × batch gradient. The ball follows the noisy arrow, not the true one.
Readouts: step number (out of 40), current loss, distance to the lowest point, and the size of the gradient noise at this step.
The noise comes from the scene's fixed seed, so Reset and every restart replay the same noise.
A run ends after 40 steps, or earlier as 'diverged' if the ball leaves the drawn surface. The current trail and the saved comparison path each hold at most 40 points.
limitations: Real losses involve many weights, flat regions and multiple dips. This single smooth bowl only shows the basic effects of step size and noise.
Single steps don't always lower the loss. With small batches the loss often rises for a step or two and only falls on average.
With batch noise and a fixed learning rate, the ball keeps jittering around the lowest point instead of settling exactly on it.
With very small learning rates, 40 steps are not enough to reach the bottom. This is intentional: it shows that tiny steps are slow.
The two arrows show the directions to move in (downhill, which is the negative gradient). They are scaled so you can see them, not drawn to true length.
plan.learningGoal: SGD steps against a gradient estimated from a small batch. The learning rate sets the step size and stability, and the batch size sets how noisy each step's direction is.
